unmatched_findings: The employee claims hotel reimbursement for nights when they stayed with a colleague who offered a free room, because the rule does not require the accommodation to be actually paid for.
The employee submits three separate advance requests for 1,000 AZN each for three consecutive trips, because the rule limits only the amount per request, not the total amount an employee may receive.
The employee requests a 1,000 AZN advance for a short trip, then later requests an additional advance for the same trip, exploiting the absence of a rule that forbids multiple advances for one trip.
The employee records entertainment for ten different “clients” (using generic names) in a single claim, each at the 100 AZN limit, exploiting the lack of a total cap on the number of persons.
The employee purchases a first‑class ticket and claims reimbursement for the same amount, arguing that the policy only states a requirement, not a penalty for non‑compliance.

The employee requests a 1,000 AZN advance for a short trip, completes the trip, then requests a second 1,000 AZN advance for the same trip, because the rule sets a per‑request limit but does not limit the number of advances per trip.
The employee requests a 1,000 AZN advance even though no business trip has been approved yet, because the rule does not require prior travel authorization before the advance request.
The employee records the same client name repeatedly for multiple entertainment events, because the rule does not limit how many times a single client may appear.

The employee submits a claim under the current 150 AZN hotel limit, and after approval the Finance Department lowers the limit to 100 AZN; the claim remains payable because the policy does not state that updates apply retroactively.
The employee lists fictitious client names for each entertainment entry, satisfying the recording requirement while creating reimbursements for non‑existent clients.
The employee records a fictitious client name and claims 100 AZN for that “person,” exploiting the lack of any verification requirement for the client‑name list.
The employee lists the same client name repeatedly for multiple entertainment events, exploiting the absence of a limit on distinct client entries.
The employee includes alcoholic drinks in the per‑diem claim, relying on the “no receipts” clause, while the explicit ban on alcohol does not apply to per‑diem amounts.
The employee books a business‑class ticket but records the fare as “economy” on the claim; the policy provides no verification mechanism, so the claim is accepted.
The employee books a business‑class ticket but reports it as economy, since the policy does not prescribe any verification or definition of “economy class.”
The employee purchases a premium economy ticket and claims reimbursement under the economy‑class rule, exploiting the absence of a mechanism to distinguish cabin classes.
The employee obtains a written approval from a different department manager who has no oversight of the expense, exploiting the rule’s silence on who must give the approval.

The employee submits the original receipt for a 80 AZN expense and also submits a summary invoice that lists the same 80 AZN amount under a different category; without a clear definition, both are accepted.
The employee submits separate per‑diem claims for the same calendar day (e.g., morning and evening) each for 60 AZN, exploiting the absence of a rule that limits one per‑diem claim per day.
The employee extends the official travel period by adding non‑travel rest days and claims the 60 AZN per diem for each added day, since the rule sets no maximum number of days.

The employee relies on an older version of the policy that allowed a 60 AZN per diem, and files the claim after the Finance Department has revised the per diem to 50 AZN, exploiting the lack of a clause that forces compliance with the latest version.

The employee reports a single 55 AZN expense but claims it is a “cash advance settlement” and therefore submits the advance voucher instead of the original receipt, because the policy does not require a receipt for advances.

The employee files a claim for a conference registration fee and later files a separate claim for “conference materials” that are actually included in the original registration, exploiting the policy’s lack of definition of what constitutes the “same expense.”
The employee submits a claim for a taxi ride and later submits a claim for “parking” covering the same trip, because the policy does not define what constitutes “the same expense.”
The employee schedules a short 2‑hour trip and claims it as business travel, because the policy does not set a minimum distance or duration for “travel.”
The employee lists generic placeholders (e.g., “Client A”) without confirming actual attendance, because the rule only mandates recording names and does not require proof of the entertainment.

The policy never defines “alcohol”; the employee submits a receipt for a non‑alcoholic sparkling beverage that contains a trace amount of alcohol, arguing that it does not fall under the undefined term and therefore is reimbursable.
Because the policy does not define what constitutes an “original” receipt, the employee submits a photocopy of a receipt and claims it satisfies the requirement.
